chapter_theme: Under the heading படைவீரர், sixteen verses on the soldier: deeds over words, loyalty that cannot join the enemy, silence about one's own valour, courage that weighs the match and is not the fool's ignorance, scorn for those who bully the weak, hide behind walls, kin or reputation, or eat the king's food without fighting, and the refusal of a daughter to a king that can end only in war.

311.reading: The verse says the worthy, having weighed the matter, close with the enemy in fierce battle whether the foe wins or they do, while those who sit within the guarded fort and rage with many words are compared to water poured into a யாப்பு.
311.nuance: தூக்கி, 'having weighed', comes before the indifference to outcome: the weighing does not decide whether to fight but is the mark of the worthy who fight anyway. யாப்பு is taken as a binding or enclosure that does not hold water, so the talk runs off; the exact object is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: water poured into a binding (an enclosure that does not hold it)

story.act: no story; talk of rage from behind the walls runs away like water poured into what cannot hold it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: big talk from safety is wasted where the worthy go out and fight

312.reading: The verse asks whether one who would give his body for his king when need comes could ever join that king's enemies, and answers with the proverb that two bulls in open enmity do not drink at one ford.

pazhamozhi.literal: two bulls do not drink water at one ford

story.act: no story; two bulls set against each other will not share a watering place

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the loyal soldier and his king's enemy cannot meet on common ground

313.reading: The verse says that when those who did great deeds stand silent and those who did nothing talk at length and blame the king, it is like the ox that, guarded from slipping, pulls the load out of the mud, while the dead weight rises where it does not.
313.nuance: The proverb's syntax is hard: வாங்கும் எருது (the ox that pulls) stands against சாக்காடு, read here as the useless, dead-weight beast, with எழாஅமை and எழல் set against each other. The general sense, that the doer is silent and the idle make the noise, is clear from lines 1-2; the image is not.

pazhamozhi.literal: where the pulling ox does not rise up, the dead weight rises

story.act: no story; an ox drawing a cart from the mud and a useless beast set side by side

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the silent doer against the complaining idler who blames the king

314.reading: The verse asks whether those who say 'we will take the battle' when their garlanded king looks at them need make the charge a common one, and says that whoever it falls to should take it up and give it, as the town is charged with the begging bowl of the Jain monks.
314.nuance: அமணர் are Jain ascetics, and the proverb assumes that the whole town feeds them, each house in turn. The application is unclear: it may mean that a battle pledged in the king's sight is everyone's charge, as the monks' bowl is the town's, or that no one may push it onto the common stock. The reading follows the second.

pazhamozhi.literal: the Jain monks' bowl is the charge of the town

story.act: no story; the alms-bowl of the Jain monks, which the townspeople fill

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a pledge made before the king is a duty for whoever it falls on

315.reading: The verse says that those who killed the strutting foe should, while others praise them, never speak of their own valour even in elation, closing with the proverb of theft that is not bundled up.
315.nuance: The praise is to come from பிறர், others; the warrior's own word about himself is what is to fall. சோரம் பொதியாதவாறு is read as stolen goods that cannot be wrapped and hidden, so the deed shows itself; it could also mean that self-praise exposes a man as a theft does. Either way the claim is that valour needs no telling.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a theft is not wrapped up

story.act: no story; something stolen that cannot be bundled out of sight

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the warrior's deed speaks without his boasting

316.reading: Addressed to the lord of the surging shore where the long dark punnai drops puffed flowers like crushed lizard eggs, the verse says the taunting talk of those who spoke does not overwhelm the great, as a jackal's howl does not reach the sea.
316.nuance: Line 1 is compressed: உரைத்தாரை மீதூரா மீக்கூற்றம் is read as the loud claims of talkers that do not rise above their object. The shore address is the akam style used for a counsel of war.
316.domain_note: the warrior or lord of the shore

pazhamozhi.literal: as a jackal's howl does not reach the sea

story.act: no story; a jackal howling at the sea

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the noise of small men does not touch the great

317.reading: Addressed to a woman with bow-like brows, the verse says that even when men are able, to rush upon the enemy in battle without being their match is harm, like striking the hand against a stone.

pazhamozhi.literal: like striking the hand on a stone

story.act: no story; a hand struck against a stone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attacking an unequal foe hurts the attacker

318.reading: The verse says that one who has entered the assembly of kings should not take fright because the strong enemy has mountain-like elephants, nor talk in turn and leave, but resolve to do one thing, for no one stills the waves before bathing in the sea.
318.nuance: உரைநடை மன்னருள் is read as the council where kings talk; நிரையுரைத்து is speaking one after another. The proverb removes the excuse of waiting for the danger to pass.
318.domain_note: a warrior in the royal council

pazhamozhi.literal: no one bathes in the sea after stilling its waves

story.act: no story; bathers do not wait for the sea to fall calm

pazhamozhi.applied_to: act despite the strong enemy instead of waiting for safety

319.reading: The verse says that petty men's soldiering is to say nothing against those who stand guard and are able, and to ride pitilessly over those who cannot resist, like a barber's razor sharpened only to cut a colocasia leaf.
319.nuance: சில்லார், 'the few' or 'the small', names a kind of man, not a number. சேப்பிலை is read as the soft leaf of the சேம்பு plant: the edge is real but spent on what offers no resistance.

pazhamozhi.literal: sharpening a barber's razor for a colocasia leaf

story.act: no story; a razor honed and then used on a soft leaf

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the courage of the petty is spent only on the weak

320.reading: The verse says that the incapable, though they shut themselves behind a fortress wall and feel secure, are caught through their fear, as a frightened bird is startled in its very body though it hides in the dark, being in the open though in darkness.

pazhamozhi.literal: in the open though in darkness

story.act: no story; a timid bird that shows itself by its own start even in the dark

pazhamozhi.applied_to: walls do not hide or save the fearful

321.reading: The verse says that those who cannot with spirit make the enemy perish in the raging battle, yet with arrogance eat their king's food as if they were doers, are those who take cloth with a கருக்கு.
321.nuance: The proverb is obscure: கருக்கு may be a jagged edge (the serrated stalk of the palmyra) or the dusk. Read as getting cloth by tearing at it or taking it in the dark, the image is of gain by false or rough means; the counsel, eating the king's food without doing his work, is clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who get cloth with a கருக்கு

story.act: no story; a man who gets cloth by an improper means

pazhamozhi.applied_to: drawing the king's pay on a show of deeds not done

322.reading: The verse says that those who turned aside from battle and were well known to have done so, saying 'our people were such men before; to whom shall we tell it', and live on food under cover of their kin's name, are like a mother who lives hidden behind her son.
322.nuance: எமர் மேலை இன்னரால் is read as an appeal to the ancestors' deeds; தமர் மறையால் is shelter behind one's kin. The proverb inverts the proper order: the mother should be the son's cover, not the son the mother's.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a mother lives with her son as her cover

story.act: no story; a mother sheltering behind her son

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the coward living on his family's earned name

323.reading: The verse says that the fool's daring, propped on his failure to perceive the many dangers, is not true daring, and that daring holds only as it is ingrained, closing with the proverb that the fear that comes of knowing is very great.
323.nuance: பொறிப்பட்டவாறு can be 'as it is stamped in' (by nature or by fate); the verse seems to say courage cannot be put on by ignorance. The proverb then admits that knowledge brings fear, so true courage is the knowing man's, holding against a fear he feels.

pazhamozhi.literal: the fear of knowing is very great

story.act: no story; the proverb states the fear that understanding brings

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the courage of ignorance is not courage

324.reading: The verse asks what want of young warriors one has who has no one stronger than himself to face, and answers that cats, though mightier than tigers, get no milk where there are no rats.
324.nuance: தன்னின் வலியானைத் தானுடையன் அல்லாதான் is read as the king with no stronger foe; he feels no need of warriors, so their worth goes unrewarded. புலியிற் பெருந்திறல is the warriors' mightiness, said of the cats with irony.

pazhamozhi.literal: cats get no milk where there are no rats

story.act: no story; household cats are fed while they have rats to catch

pazhamozhi.applied_to: warriors are valued only while there is an enemy

325.reading: The verse says of those who are reputed to have generosity, conduct and grasping intelligence but lack the strength to march on the enemy's possessions, that the bearing of an army is better than an army.
325.nuance: The proverb may be praise or irony. Read with lines 1-3, such men serve only as the look of a force, its படைத்தகைமை, not its striking power; it is uncertain whether that is meant as their use or their shame.

pazhamozhi.literal: an army's bearing is better than the army

story.act: no story; the proverb weighs an army's appearance against its strength

pazhamozhi.applied_to: men of good name but no drive to attack serve only as display

326.reading: The verse says that if the king demands the young girl with eyes like two carp, even her brothers will not consent, and there is nothing but the sweet sight of them swinging their mighty shoulders as they declare battle, for no one salts a raw plantain.
326.nuance: This is the Sangam theme of a girl refused to a king, and war that follows, told here as a certainty with a kitchen proverb. தன்னையர் are the girl's elder brothers, not her father. The proverb is read as 'there is no other treatment for it'; the exact sense of salting a plantain is not sure.
326.domain_note: the girl's kin as warriors against a king

pazhamozhi.literal: no one rubs salt into a raw plantain

story.act: no story; a kitchen practice that is not done

pazhamozhi.applied_to: war is the only answer when a king demands a daughter of a proud house

links.note: Pazhamozhi 311 praises the worthy who, having weighed it, meet the foe whether they or the enemy win; 317 calls attacking without being the enemy's match a harm, like striking a stone.
links.teaches: Read together, the weighing in 311 does not license fighting any foe: courage indifferent to outcome is admired, but 317 bars the charge against a clearly superior enemy, so the chapter separates accepting risk from courting certain defeat.

links.note: Both set the silent fighter against the talker: in 311 those who rage within the fort with many words, in 313 the idle who talk and blame the king while the doers stand silent.
links.teaches: The pair shows the chapter's double charge against talk in war: it is wasted when made from safety, and it becomes slander when the talker turns it on the king.

links.note: Kural 764 makes an army one that cannot be turned by subversion (அறைபோகாது); Pazhamozhi 312 asks whether one who would give his body for the king could join his enemies.
links.teaches: The couplet names the quality, incorruptibility, as a property of the army; Pazhamozhi grounds it in the single soldier's willingness to die, so loyalty becomes the consequence of a readiness to give the body rather than a separate virtue.
links.list_adds: its two-bulls proverb gives a reason the couplet lacks: enmity so settled that the two cannot even share a ford, so desertion is shown as unnatural rather than only forbidden.

links.note: Naladiyar 346 says the excellent never speak a boastful word even with an emperor's wealth; Pazhamozhi 315 asks the warrior who has killed the strutting foe not to tell his own valour.
links.teaches: The quatrain's restraint concerns wealth and the base man's swagger; Pazhamozhi carries it to the battlefield, where the deed is real and the praise of others is due, so silence is asked even of one who has earned praise.
links.list_adds: it moves the rule from wealth to valour and gives the reason in a proverb, that the deed shows itself as a theft cannot be bundled, where the quatrain gives only the contrast of excellent and base.

links.note: Kural 473 says many who did not know their strength rose on zeal and were broken midway; Pazhamozhi 317 says that even capable men who rush on an unequal foe come to harm, like a hand struck on stone.
links.teaches: The couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength; Pazhamozhi adds that being able (ஆற்றுவாரேனும்) is not enough, since what counts is the match (நிகர்) with the enemy, so the weighing is relative, not absolute.
links.list_adds: it shifts the measure from the self's strength to the comparison with the enemy and gives the image of injury to the striker, which the couplet's broken-midway leaves general.

links.note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one spoke is hard; Pazhamozhi 318 asks the man in the council of kings not to talk in turn and leave but to resolve to act, undeterred by the enemy's elephants.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the difficulty in doing; Pazhamozhi names what makes doing hard in war, fear of a strong enemy, and refuses the wait for a safer moment, so resolve is tied to accepting risk.
links.list_adds: it sets the contrast in the royal council before war and adds the waves proverb, which answers the excuse of waiting that the couplet does not consider.

links.note: Kural 772 says carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than an arrow that hit a hare; Pazhamozhi 319 scorns petty men who keep quiet before the strong and overrun the weak.
links.teaches: Both measure valour by its target rather than its success, and Pazhamozhi names the opposite type the couplet only implies: the man who chooses hares, silent before the guard and pitiless to the helpless.
links.list_adds: it adds the social side the couplet lacks, the bully's two faces toward strong and weak, and the razor image of sharpness wasted on what offers no resistance.

links.note: Kural 534 says the fearful have no fortress; Pazhamozhi 320 says the incapable are caught through fear though shut behind walls, like a timid bird that betrays itself in the dark.
links.teaches: The couplet states that walls do not help the fearful; Pazhamozhi shows how, since fear itself gives them away, as the bird's start reveals it, so the failure is exposure from within, not weak defences.
links.list_adds: it supplies the mechanism through the bird image, the fear that makes its holder visible, which the couplet's flat 'no fortress' does not give.

links.note: Kural 428 calls not fearing what should be feared folly and fearing it the work of the knowing; Pazhamozhi 323 denies that the fool's daring, resting on ignorance of dangers, is daring, and grants that knowing brings great fear.
links.teaches: The couplet makes fear a mark of wisdom in general; Pazhamozhi carries it to the soldier and draws the hard consequence, that the brave man is one who knows the danger and so feels the fear, making courage a matter of holding against it rather than lacking it.
links.list_adds: it moves the claim into the soldier's domain and turns it against a kind of courage, ruling out the fearless fool as brave, which the couplet does not say.

links.note: Kural 768 says that even without striking power or endurance an army gains stature by its படைத்தகை; Pazhamozhi 325 uses the same word for men of good name who lack the drive to march on the enemy.
links.teaches: The couplet treats bearing as a real asset of a weak army; Pazhamozhi turns it on men, so that bearing without ஊற்றம் becomes their measure, and the concession reads, on this reading, as a limited or ironic praise.
links.list_adds: its list of generosity, conduct and intelligence as the virtues of reputation sets the warrior's drive apart from them, showing that the civil virtues do not make a fighting man.

links.note: Purananuru 341 tells of a father who will not give his young daughter even when the king pleads and takes up arms with his tiger-like kin, torn between her wedding tomorrow and death; Pazhamozhi 326 says even the girl's brothers will refuse the king and the only outcome is battle.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem holds the refusal as a tragic choice and grieves for the town's beauty; the ethics verse keeps the heroic memory but removes the dilemma, so the refusal becomes a fixed rule of a proud house and war the only remedy, said with a kitchen proverb.
